## Core Principles

### I. Domain-Driven Business Rules
The invoice lifecycle and approval decisions MUST live in the domain layer, not in controllers or UI code. The ApprovalService owns the valid transitions among Draft, Pending Approval, Approved, and Rejected, and all rule changes MUST be implemented there before any API or web behavior is updated.

This keeps the business policy explicit, testable, and consistent across the API and the demo UI. Controllers are callers of the domain, not independent sources of business logic.

### II. Role-Secured API Access
Every API action MUST require an authenticated session and MUST enforce role-based authorization. Destructive actions are Admin-only, approval actions require Approver or Admin, and no endpoint may bypass this rule in the name of convenience or demo speed.

The role model is part of the application contract. If a request changes the invoice state, the role check must be explicit and verifiable in code and tests.

### III. Test-First Delivery
Every behavior change MUST be covered by tests before implementation is considered complete. Domain rules are validated with xUnit tests, and user-visible flows are validated with Playwright when the change affects the approval workflow, authorization, or web experience.

A feature is not complete when it merely runs locally; it is complete only when the relevant tests exercise the changed behavior and fail before the fix and pass after it.

### IV. Verified User Experience
The web app and API are a single workflow and MUST be tested as a product, not as isolated components. Changes to invoice submission, approval, rejection, or role-based access MUST verify the observable outcome from the userΓÇÖs perspective as well as the service logic.

This protects against regression where the domain passes but the user flow breaks, and it keeps the demo usable for live AI-in-SDLC presentations.

### V. Simplicity and Change Safety
The project MUST stay intentionally small, understandable, and easy to review. The app uses a .NET 8 API, a plain web UI, and an in-memory store because they are sufficient for the demo and reduce operational complexity; broader infrastructure or premature abstraction is not allowed unless a project requirement clearly demands it.

Simplicity is a governance rule, not a preference. It reduces confusion, makes change impact obvious, and keeps the app safe to evolve during demos and exercises.

## Operational Standards

The invoice approval demo MUST remain aligned with the following standards:

- The domain project owns business rules and repository contracts; the API project owns controllers, authentication, and UI assets.
- Repositories are interfaces in the domain project with in-memory implementations in the API project for local, single-process execution.
- Controllers MUST inherit from ApiControllerBase and route using the pattern api/[controller].
- Request records are declared in the controller and used only to shape API input; no business logic is allowed there.
- All new rules or endpoints require tests using the existing FakeInvoiceRepository and the projectΓÇÖs xUnit and Playwright conventions.
- Naming MUST be explicit and readable; one-letter variables and vague flag parameters are prohibited.
- Demo credentials are only for local use and MUST never be treated as real production credentials or committed as sensitive secrets.

## Delivery Workflow

Changes to this project MUST follow the repository workflow described in AGENTS.md and the project README:

- Business rules are implemented in the domain project before the API layer is updated.
- Authentication and authorization requirements are enforced before endpoints are considered complete.
- Tests are required for every new rule, endpoint, or regression fix.
- Manual verification is expected for the approval flow and role check behavior in the browser when a user-facing change is made.
- Pull requests and code review MUST confirm that the change respects the domain boundary, the role model, and the simple architecture of the app.

## Governance

This Constitution supersedes informal practices for this repository. All project changes MUST be evaluated against it before being considered complete.

Amendments require a clear rationale, updated versioning, and a review of the impacted principles and workflow sections. The project MUST record the change in this constitution, note the reason for the amendment, and retain a traceable history of the decision.

Versioning MUST follow semantic versioning: MAJOR changes remove or redefine governance rules in a backward-incompatible way, MINOR changes add or materially expand a principle or section, and PATCH changes clarify wording or refine non-semantic guidance. A change that adds a governance requirement or materially narrows allowed behavior is a MAJOR or MINOR change based on impact.

Compliance review is mandatory before a change is considered ready. Reviewers MUST verify that the behavior, tests, and documentation remain aligned with the domain rule, the role model, and the projectΓÇÖs simplicity standard.

## Core Principles

### I. Domain-Driven Business Rules
The invoice lifecycle and approval decisions MUST live in the domain layer, not in controllers or UI code. The ApprovalService owns the valid transitions among Draft, Pending Approval, Approved, and Rejected, and all rule changes MUST be implemented there before any API or web behavior is updated.

This keeps the business policy explicit, testable, and consistent across the API and the demo UI. Controllers are callers of the domain, not independent sources of business logic.

### II. Role-Secured API Access
Every API action MUST require an authenticated session and MUST enforce role-based authorization. Destructive actions are Admin-only, approval actions require Approver or Admin, and no endpoint may bypass this rule in the name of convenience or demo speed.

The role model is part of the application contract. If a request changes the invoice state, the role check must be explicit and verifiable in code and tests.

### III. Test-First Delivery
Every behavior change MUST be covered by tests before implementation is considered complete. Domain rules are validated with xUnit tests, and user-visible flows are validated with Playwright when the change affects the approval workflow, authorization, or web experience.

A feature is not complete when it merely runs locally; it is complete only when the relevant tests exercise the changed behavior and fail before the fix and pass after it.

### IV. Verified User Experience
The web app and API are a single workflow and MUST be tested as a product, not as isolated components. Changes to invoice submission, approval, rejection, or role-based access MUST verify the observable outcome from the userΓÇÖs perspective as well as the service logic.

This protects against regression where the domain passes but the user flow breaks, and it keeps the demo usable for live AI-in-SDLC presentations.

### V. Simplicity and Change Safety
The project MUST stay intentionally small, understandable, and easy to review. The app uses a .NET 8 API, a plain web UI, and an in-memory store because they are sufficient for the demo and reduce operational complexity; broader infrastructure or premature abstraction is not allowed unless a project requirement clearly demands it.

Simplicity is a governance rule, not a preference. It reduces confusion, makes change impact obvious, and keeps the app safe to evolve during demos and exercises.

## Operational Standards

The invoice approval demo MUST remain aligned with the following standards:

- The domain project owns business rules and repository contracts; the API project owns controllers, authentication, and UI assets.
- Repositories are interfaces in the domain project with in-memory implementations in the API project for local, single-process execution.
- Controllers MUST inherit from ApiControllerBase and route using the conventional api/<controller> pattern.
- Request records are declared in the controller and used only to shape API input; no business logic is allowed there.
- All new rules or endpoints require tests using the existing FakeInvoiceRepository and the projectΓÇÖs xUnit and Playwright conventions.
- Naming MUST be explicit and readable; one-letter variables and vague flag parameters are prohibited.
- Demo credentials are only for local use and MUST never be treated as real production credentials or committed as sensitive secrets.

## Delivery Workflow

Changes to this project MUST follow the repository workflow described in AGENTS.md and the project README:

- Business rules are implemented in the domain project before the API layer is updated.
- Authentication and authorization requirements are enforced before endpoints are considered complete.
- Tests are required for every new rule, endpoint, or regression fix.
- Manual verification is expected for the approval flow and role check behavior in the browser when a user-facing change is made.
- Pull requests and code review MUST confirm that the change respects the domain boundary, the role model, and the simple architecture of the app.

**Feature Branch**: `001-approval-workflow`

**Created**: 2026-10-22

**Status**: Draft

**Input**: User description: "Managers may finally approve invoices up to 50,000. Directors may finally approve invoices up to 500,000. For invoices above 500,000, a Manager provides the first-stage approval, and a different Director provides the second-stage approval that finalizes the invoice. The same user cannot satisfy both approval stages. Invalid approval attempts must return a clear reason and leave the invoice unchanged."

## User Scenarios & Testing *(mandatory)*

### User Story 1 - Routine invoice approval by a manager (Priority: P1)

A manager needs to finalize an invoice that is within the manager approval limit without escalating to a director. The workflow must be clear, fast, and auditable so the approver can complete the action confidently and understand the result.

**Why this priority**: This is the primary business path for day-to-day invoice approval and must work consistently before any exception workflow is considered.

**Independent Test**: A manager can approve an invoice below the manager threshold and the invoice moves to a final approved state with a clear decision record.

**Acceptance Scenarios**:

1. **Given** an invoice in Pending Approval with an amount at or below 50,000, **When** a manager submits a final approval, **Then** the invoice is approved and the approver identity is recorded.
2. **Given** an invoice in Pending Approval with an amount above 50,000, **When** a manager attempts a final approval, **Then** the request is rejected with a clear reason and the invoice remains unchanged.

---

### User Story 2 - Director approval for larger invoices (Priority: P1)

A director needs to approve invoices that are within the director threshold. The process must ensure that only the correct role can finalize these higher-value transactions and that any invalid attempt is explained clearly.

**Why this priority**: These approvals carry higher financial risk and require explicit role-based controls to protect governance and avoid accidental over-approval.

**Independent Test**: A director can approve an invoice at or below 500,000 and it is finalized only when the invoice is eligible for director approval.

**Acceptance Scenarios**:

1. **Given** an invoice in Pending Approval with an amount between 50,001 and 500,000, **When** a director submits a final approval, **Then** the invoice is approved and the final approver is recorded.
2. **Given** an invoice in Pending Approval with an amount above 500,000, **When** a director attempts a final approval without the required manager stage, **Then** the request is rejected with a clear reason and no state change occurs.

---

### User Story 3 - Multi-stage approval for very large invoices (Priority: P1)

A very large invoice requires two approval stages: a manager provides the first-stage approval, and a different director provides the final approval. The system must enforce both steps and prevent the same user from satisfying both stages.

**Why this priority**: This is the highest-risk scenario and requires explicit separation of duties to maintain approval integrity.

**Independent Test**: A manager and a different director can complete the required stages for a high-value invoice, while an invalid same-user or missing second-stage attempt is blocked.

**Acceptance Scenarios**:

1. **Given** an invoice above 500,000 that is pending stage-based approval, **When** a manager provides the first-stage approval and a different director provides the second-stage final approval, **Then** the invoice is finalized successfully.
2. **Given** an invoice above 500,000, **When** the same user attempts to satisfy both stages, **Then** the request is rejected and the invoice remains unchanged.
3. **Given** an invoice above 500,000 with a single approval step missing, **When** a user attempts to finalize the invoice, **Then** the system returns a clear reason and does not mutate the invoice state.

---

### User Story 4 - Invalid approval attempts and clear reasons (Priority: P2)

An approver needs immediate feedback when the approval action is invalid. The system must explain the reason and preserve the invoice state so that users can correct their action without uncertainty.

**Why this priority**: Clear reasons reduce confusion and protect operational trust in the approval process.

**Independent Test**: Invalid approval actions return a message that explains the rule violation and leave the invoice unchanged.

**Acceptance Scenarios**:

1. **Given** an invoice that is not pending approval, **When** an approver attempts to approve or reject it, **Then** the system returns a clear reason and leaves the invoice state unchanged.
2. **Given** a missing or blank reason for a rejection, **When** the rejection is submitted, **Then** the system returns a clear reason and does not save the decision.

---

### Edge Cases

- What happens when an invoice amount is exactly 50,000 or exactly 500,000?
- How does the system handle approval attempts from the same user in a two-stage approval flow?
- What happens when a manager or director attempts to approve an invoice in a different status than Pending Approval?
- How does the system respond when a second-stage approval is attempted before the first-stage approval is recorded?

## Requirements *(mandatory)*

### Functional Requirements

- **FR-001**: The system MUST allow managers to provide a final approval for invoices up to and including 50,000.
- **FR-002**: The system MUST allow directors to provide a final approval for invoices up to and including 500,000.
- **FR-003**: The system MUST require a two-stage approval flow for invoices above 500,000, with a manager completing the first stage and a different director completing the final stage.
- **FR-004**: The system MUST prevent the same user from satisfying both approval stages for the same invoice.
- **FR-005**: The system MUST reject invalid approval attempts with a clear, user-facing reason when the invoice is not eligible for the requested action.
- **FR-006**: The system MUST leave the invoice unchanged when an approval attempt is invalid.
- **FR-007**: The system MUST record the final approver identity and decision outcome in a manner that supports review and audit decisions.
- **FR-008**: The system MUST preserve the existing authentication and authorization model while enforcing the approval workflow rules.
- **FR-009**: The system MUST maintain a clear distinction between approval and rejection outcomes so that final states remain unambiguous.

### Key Entities *(include if feature involves data)*

- **Invoice**: The business record being reviewed, including amount, status, and decision history.
- **Approver**: A person or role-based actor who can take part in an approval action.
- **Approval Stage**: A specific step in the approval sequence, including first-stage manager approval and final director approval.
- **Approval Decision**: The final outcome of the invoice review, including approval, rejection, the actor, and the reason if applicable.

## Success Criteria *(mandatory)*

### Measurable Outcomes

- **SC-001**: 100% of approval attempts for invoices at or below the configured thresholds follow the correct approval role and final outcome rules.
- **SC-002**: 100% of invalid approval attempts result in a clear reason and no invoice state mutation.
- **SC-003**: 100% of multi-stage approvals above 500,000 require distinct approver identities across the required stages.
- **SC-004**: Users can understand the approval outcome and reason without needing to inspect implementation internals or hidden code paths.
- **SC-005**: The workflow remains aligned with the projectΓÇÖs existing role-based security and domain-layer governance requirements.

## Assumptions

- The approval policy is defined by the projectΓÇÖs business rules rather than by ad hoc controller logic.
- Existing role-based authentication and authorization rules remain in effect for all approval actions.
- Approval decisions are evaluated against the invoice amount and current status before any approval is accepted.
- The detailed feature specification may refine the user-facing labels and messages, but the approval invariants remain non-negotiable.
- The system can be reviewed and validated through the existing unit and workflow test conventions already used in the repository.

A director needs to approve invoices that are within the director threshold. The process must ensure that only the correct role can finalize these higher-value transactions and that any invalid attempt is explained clearly.

children.text: **Input**: User description: "Managers may finally approve invoices up to 50,000. Directors may finally approve invoices up to 500,000. For invoices above 500,000, a Manager provides the first-stage approval, and a different Director provides the second-stage approval that finalizes the invoice. The same user cannot satisfy both approval stages. Invalid approval attempts must return a clear reason and leave the invoice unchanged."
### User Story 1 - Routine invoice approval by a manager (Priority: P1)

A manager needs to finalize an invoice that is within the manager approval limit without escalating to a director. The workflow must be clear, fast, and auditable so the approver can complete the action confidently and understand the result.
**Why this priority**: This is the primary business path for day-to-day invoice approval and must work consistently before any exception workflow is considered.
**Independent Test**: A manager can approve an invoice below the manager threshold and the invoice moves to a final approved state with a clear decision record.
1. **Given** an invoice in Pending Approval with an amount at or below 50,000, **When** a manager submits a final approval, **Then** the invoice is approved and the approver identity is recorded.

2. **Given** an invoice in Pending Approval with an amount above 50,000, **When** a manager attempts a final approval, **Then** the request is rejected with a clear reason and the invoice remains unchanged.
### User Story 2 - Director approval for larger invoices (Priority: P1)

A director needs to approve invoices that are within the director threshold. The process must ensure that only the correct role can finalize these higher-value transactions and that any invalid attempt is explained clearly.
**Why this priority**: These approvals carry higher financial risk and require explicit role-based controls to protect governance and avoid accidental over-approval.
**Independent Test**: A director can approve an invoice at or below 500,000 and it is finalized only when the invoice is eligible for director approval.

1. **Given** an invoice in Pending Approval with an amount between 50,001 and 500,000, **When** a director submits a final approval, **Then** the invoice is approved and the final approver is recorded.

2. **Given** an invoice in Pending Approval with an amount above 500,000, **When** a director attempts a final approval without the required manager stage, **Then** the request is rejected with a clear reason and no state change occurs.
### User Story 3 - Multi-stage approval for very large invoices (Priority: P1)

A very large invoice requires two approval stages: a manager provides the first-stage approval, and a different director provides the final approval. The system must enforce both steps and prevent the same user from satisfying both stages.
**Why this priority**: This is the highest-risk scenario and requires explicit separation of duties to maintain approval integrity.
**Independent Test**: A manager and a different director can complete the required stages for a high-value invoice, while an invalid same-user or missing second-stage attempt is blocked.

1. **Given** an invoice above 500,000 that is pending stage-based approval, **When** a manager provides the first-stage approval and a different director provides the second-stage final approval, **Then** the invoice is finalized successfully.
2. **Given** an invoice above 500,000, **When** the same user attempts to satisfy both stages, **Then** the request is rejected and the invoice remains unchanged.

3. **Given** an invoice above 500,000 with a single approval step missing, **When** a user attempts to finalize the invoice, **Then** the system returns a clear reason and does not mutate the invoice state.
### User Story 4 - Invalid approval attempts and clear reasons (Priority: P2)
An approver needs immediate feedback when the approval action is invalid. The system must explain the reason and preserve the invoice state so that users can correct their action without uncertainty.
**Why this priority**: Clear reasons reduce confusion and protect operational trust in the approval process.
**Independent Test**: Invalid approval actions return a message that explains the rule violation and leave the invoice unchanged.
1. **Given** an invoice that is not pending approval, **When** an approver attempts to approve or reject it, **Then** the system returns a clear reason and leaves the invoice state unchanged.
2. **Given** a missing or blank reason for a rejection, **When** the rejection is submitted, **Then** the system returns a clear reason and does not save the decision.
- What happens when an invoice amount is exactly 50,000 or exactly 500,000?
- How does the system handle approval attempts from the same user in a two-stage approval flow?
- What happens when a manager or director attempts to approve an invoice in a different status than Pending Approval?
- How does the system respond when a second-stage approval is attempted before the first-stage approval is recorded?
- **FR-001**: The system MUST allow managers to provide a final approval for invoices up to and including 50,000.
- **FR-002**: The system MUST allow directors to provide a final approval for invoices up to and including 500,000.
- **FR-003**: The system MUST require a two-stage approval flow for invoices above 500,000, with a manager completing the first stage and a different director completing the final stage.
- **FR-004**: The system MUST prevent the same user from satisfying both approval stages for the same invoice.
- **FR-005**: The system MUST reject invalid approval attempts with a clear, user-facing reason when the invoice is not eligible for the requested action.
- **FR-006**: The system MUST leave the invoice unchanged when an approval attempt is invalid.
- **FR-007**: The system MUST record the final approver identity and decision outcome in a manner that supports review and audit decisions.
- **FR-008**: The system MUST preserve the existing authentication and authorization model while enforcing the approval workflow rules.
- **FR-009**: The system MUST maintain a clear distinction between approval and rejection outcomes so that final states remain unambiguous.
### Key Entities *(include if feature involves data)*
- **Invoice**: The business record being reviewed, including amount, status, and decision history.
- **Approver**: A person or role-based actor who can take part in an approval action.
- **Approval Stage**: A specific step in the approval sequence, including first-stage manager approval and final director approval.
- **Approval Decision**: The final outcome of the invoice review, including approval, rejection, the actor, and the reason if applicable.
- **SC-001**: 100% of approval attempts for invoices at or below the configured thresholds follow the correct approval role and final outcome rules.
- **SC-002**: 100% of invalid approval attempts result in a clear reason and no invoice state mutation.
- **SC-003**: 100% of multi-stage approvals above 500,000 require distinct approver identities across the required stages.
- **SC-004**: Users can understand the approval outcome and reason without needing to inspect implementation internals or hidden code paths.
- **SC-005**: The workflow remains aligned with the projectΓÇÖs existing role-based security and domain-layer governance requirements.
- The approval policy is defined by the projectΓÇÖs business rules rather than by ad hoc controller logic.
- Existing role-based authentication and authorization rules remain in effect for all approval actions.
- Approval decisions are evaluated against the invoice amount and current status before any approval is accepted.

children.text: **Input**: User description: "Managers may finally approve invoices up to 50,000. Directors may finally approve invoices up to 500,000. For invoices above 500,000, a Manager provides the first-stage approval, and a different Director provides the second-stage approval that finalizes the invoice. The same user cannot satisfy both approval stages. Invalid approval attempts must return a clear reason and leave the invoice unchanged."
### User Story 1 - Routine invoice approval by a manager (Priority: P1)

A manager needs to finalize an invoice that is within the manager approval limit without escalating to a director. The workflow must be clear, auditable, and easy to verify when the amount is at the threshold boundary.
**Why this priority**: This is the primary business path for daily invoice processing and must behave correctly at exact threshold boundaries before any exception path is considered.
**Independent Test**: A manager can finalize an invoice exactly at the manager limit and the invoice records a clear final decision without ambiguity.
1. **Given** an invoice in Pending Approval with an amount of exactly 50,000, **When** a manager submits a final approval, **Then** the invoice is approved and the approving manager is recorded.

2. **Given** an invoice in Pending Approval with an amount of 50,001, **When** a manager submits a final approval, **Then** the request is rejected with a clear reason and the invoice remains unchanged.
3. **Given** an invoice in Pending Approval with an amount below 50,000, **When** a manager submits a final approval, **Then** the invoice is approved as the managerΓÇÖs final decision.
### User Story 2 - Director approval for larger invoices (Priority: P1)

A director needs to finalize invoices that are within the director approval limit. The process must ensure that only the correct role can decide at that threshold and that invalid role attempts are rejected without mutating the invoice.
**Why this priority**: Director approvals involve larger values and require explicit role enforcement to avoid unauthorized final decisions.
**Independent Test**: A director can finalize an invoice at 500,000, while non-director users or out-of-range approvals are rejected with a clear reason and no invoice mutation.

1. **Given** an invoice in Pending Approval with an amount of exactly 500,000, **When** a director submits a final approval, **Then** the invoice is approved and the director is recorded as the final approver.

2. **Given** an invoice in Pending Approval with an amount above 500,000, **When** a director attempts a final approval without the required first-stage manager approval, **Then** the request is rejected with a clear reason and the invoice remains unchanged.

3. **Given** an invoice in Pending Approval with an amount above 500,000, **When** a user without the Director role attempts the final approval, **Then** the request is rejected with a clear reason and no invoice fields are changed.
### User Story 3 - Multi-stage approval for very large invoices (Priority: P1)

A very large invoice requires a two-stage approval path: a manager completes the first stage, and a different director completes the second stage to finalize the invoice. The same user cannot satisfy both stages, and rejected attempts must not alter approval history.
**Why this priority**: This is the highest-risk approval scenario, and it requires explicit separation of duties and strict state preservation to prevent invalid progression.

**Independent Test**: A manager and a different director can complete the required stages for a large invoice, while same-user, missing-stage, or out-of-order stage attempts are rejected without mutation.

1. **Given** an invoice above 500,000 that is pending a two-stage approval flow, **When** a manager records the first-stage approval and a different director records the second-stage final approval, **Then** the invoice is finalized successfully and the stage history reflects the two different approvers.

2. **Given** an invoice above 500,000, **When** a second-stage approval is attempted before the first-stage manager approval is recorded, **Then** the attempt is rejected with a clear reason and the invoice remains unchanged.

3. **Given** an invoice above 500,000, **When** the same user attempts to satisfy both stages, **Then** the second-stage attempt is rejected and the invoiceΓÇÖs status, stage records, final approver, decision timestamp, and decision note history remain unchanged.

4. **Given** an invoice above 500,000, **When** the required manager stage is recorded but a different director fails to complete final approval, **Then** the invoice remains pending and the prior stage record remains intact until a valid final approval is submitted.
### User Story 4 - Invalid approval attempts, lifecycle errors, and state preservation (Priority: P2)

An approver needs immediate feedback whenever the approval action is invalid. The system must explain the reason, preserve the invoice state, and keep rejection behavior distinct from approval so the business can correct the action confidently.

**Why this priority**: Invalid approval attempts are high-risk from a governance perspective because they can create confusion, duplicate decisions, or silent state drift if they are not clearly blocked.
**Independent Test**: Approval and rejection attempts that do not meet the current lifecycle, role, or data requirements are rejected without mutating the invoiceΓÇÖs recorded state.

1. **Given** an invoice that is not in Pending Approval, **When** an approver attempts to approve or reject it, **Then** the system rejects the attempt with a clear reason and preserves the invoiceΓÇÖs status, approver, timestamp, and decision note history.

2. **Given** an invoice that has already received a final approval or rejection, **When** a repeated approval or rejection attempt is submitted, **Then** the system rejects the attempt and leaves the invoice decision unchanged.
3. **Given** an invoice pending approval, **When** a user submits a rejection without a reason, **Then** the system rejects the rejection without saving a decision or mutating the invoice.

4. **Given** a user without the required role for the current stage, **When** they attempt to complete that approval stage, **Then** the action is rejected with a clear reason and no invoice fields are changed.

5. **Given** a rejected approval attempt, **When** the system evaluates the resulting state, **Then** the invoice retains the same status, approval-stage records, final approver, decision timestamp, and decision note/history that existed before the rejected attempt.

- How does the system handle repeated approval attempts after a final decision has already been recorded?
- What happens when the same user attempts to satisfy both stages of a two-stage approval for an amount above 500,000?
- How does the system respond when a second-stage approval is attempted before the first-stage manager approval exists?
- What does ΓÇ£unchangedΓÇ¥ mean for the invoice when a rejected attempt occurs?
- **FR-001**: The system MUST allow a Manager to provide a final approval for an invoice of exactly 50,000.
- **FR-002**: The system MUST reject a Manager final approval attempt for any invoice above 50,000.
- **FR-003**: The system MUST allow a Director to provide a final approval for an invoice of exactly 500,000.
- **FR-004**: The system MUST reject a Director final approval attempt for any invoice above 500,000 unless the required Manager first-stage approval has already been recorded.
- **FR-005**: The system MUST require a Manager first-stage approval before a Director can finalize an invoice above 500,000.
- **FR-006**: The system MUST require a different approver identity for the final Director stage than the Manager who completed the earlier stage.
- **FR-007**: The system MUST reject any approval attempt where the same user would satisfy both approval stages for the same invoice.
- **FR-008**: The system MUST reject any approval attempt by users without the required role for that stage, with a clear reason and no invoice mutation.
- **FR-009**: The system MUST reject approval attempts against invoices that are not in Pending Approval without mutating the invoice.
- **FR-010**: The system MUST reject repeated approval or rejection attempts after a final decision has already been recorded without changing the recorded decision.
- **FR-011**: The system MUST reject any rejection attempt that does not include a valid reason without saving the decision.

- **FR-012**: For any rejected approval or rejection attempt, the system MUST preserve the invoiceΓÇÖs status, approval-stage records, final approver, decision timestamp, and decision note/history that existed before the rejected attempt.
- **FR-013**: The system MUST maintain a clear distinction between approval and rejection outcomes so that final states remain unambiguous.
- **FR-014**: The system MUST preserve the existing authentication and authorization model while enforcing the approval workflow rules.
### Key Entities *(include if feature involves data)*
- **Invoice**: The business record being reviewed, including amount, status, approval stages, and decision history.
- **Approver**: A person or role-based actor who can take part in an approval action.
- **Approval Stage**: A specific step in the approval sequence, including the Manager first-stage approval and the Director final-stage approval.
- **Approval Decision**: The final outcome of the invoice review, including approval, rejection, the actor, and the reason when applicable.
- **SC-001**: 100% of Manager final approval attempts at 50,000 are accepted, and 100% of Manager final approval attempts above 50,000 are rejected with a clear reason and no invoice mutation.

- **SC-002**: 100% of Director final approval attempts at 500,000 are accepted, and 100% of Director final approval attempts above 500,000 are rejected unless a valid Manager first-stage approval has already been recorded.
- **SC-003**: 100% of approval flows above 500,000 require a Manager first-stage approval and a different Director second-stage approval before finalization occurs.
- **SC-004**: 100% of same-user, out-of-order, or missing-stage approval attempts are rejected, and the invoice remains unchanged for every rejected attempt.

- **SC-005**: 100% of invalid-role approval attempts are rejected with a clear reason and do not modify the invoice status, stage records, final approver, decision timestamp, or decision note/history.
- **SC-006**: 100% of repeated approval attempts after a final decision and blank rejection attempts are rejected without changing the recorded decision.
- **SC-007**: Users can understand the approval outcome and the reason for rejection without inspecting hidden implementation details or backend state not exposed by the workflow rules.
- The approval policy is defined by the projectΓÇÖs business rules rather than by ad hoc controller logic.
- Existing role-based authentication and authorization rules remain in effect for all approval actions.
- Approval decisions are evaluated against the invoice amount and current status before any approval is accepted.

- A rejected approval attempt is considered unsuccessful only when the invoice state remains unchanged in all fields relevant to approval status, stage records, final approver, decision timestamp, and decision note/history.

## Summary

This feature adds explicit approval thresholds and separation-of-duties rules for invoices in the existing ASP.NET Core demo. The implementation must keep the invoice lifecycle and approval invariants in the domain layer so the API layer remains a thin adapter over a validated business service. The work is split into two stages: first the single-stage manager/director decision rules at 50,000 and 500,000, then the two-stage path for amounts above 500,000, with unit tests driving each rule and a Playwright workflow test validating the end-user flow.

## Technical Context

**Language/Version**: C# / .NET 8, ASP.NET Core Web API

**Primary Dependencies**: xUnit, Playwright, existing in-memory repository and session-based role auth

**Storage**: In-memory repository in the API project; domain contracts remain interface-based and repository-agnostic

**Testing**: xUnit for domain/unit tests; Playwright for end-to-end role-based workflow validation; Stryker.NET for mutation testing using the repo-approved pinned version

**Target Platform**: Local demo web app and automated tests in the repository workspace

**Project Type**: Web service + static UI demo

**Performance Goals**: no throughput target beyond synchronous local demo behavior; correctness and state preservation are the primary constraints

**Constraints**: approval rules must remain in InvoiceApp.Domain; controllers must not encode business logic; all rejected attempts must preserve state; existing auth/session model must remain intact

**Scale/Scope**: small demo app with a single invoice approval workflow and a small set of role-based scenarios

## Constitution Check

*Gate status: PASS before implementation, with explicit compliance checks to re-run after design and before completion.*

- Business logic stays in InvoiceApp.Domain; controllers remain request shapers and keep using ApiControllerBase and RequireRole enforcement.
- Test-first development is enforced by adding failing xUnit tests for each approval threshold and invalid-attempt case before implementation.
- Approval correctness is preserved through explicit threshold checks, separation-of-duties rules, and no-mutation semantics for rejected attempts.
- API and security consistency remains intact because session-based role enforcement continues to live in the existing auth model.
- Minimal scope is maintained by reusing the existing ApprovalService, repository contract, and test patterns rather than introducing new abstractions or unrelated refactoring.
- Verification is required through `dotnet test backend/InvoiceApp.sln`, Playwright validation, and mutation testing before considering the feature complete.

## Implementation Phases

### Phase 0: Test-first domain specification

Goal: lock down the approval invariants before any production code changes.

Planned work:
- Add failing unit tests in [backend/tests/InvoiceApp.Tests/ApprovalServiceTests.cs](backend/tests/InvoiceApp.Tests/ApprovalServiceTests.cs) for the exact threshold boundaries.
- Cover the manager single-stage path at 50,000 and 50,001.
- Cover the director single-stage path at 500,000 and above 500,000 without the required manager stage.
- Cover invalid-role attempts and blank rejection reasons.
- Cover same-user stage attempts and out-of-order stage attempts for the >500,000 flow.

Exit criteria:
- Tests fail before implementation because the new business rules are not yet present.
- Each test names the exact invariant it protects.
- No rule is accepted without a failing test demonstrating the expected behavior.

### Phase 1: Single-stage approval rules

Goal: implement the path for manager and director approvals that do not require a second stage.

Planned logic in `ApprovalService`:
- Manager approval is valid for amounts `<= 50,000` and rejected above 50,000.
- Director approval is valid for amounts `> 50,000` and `<= 500,000`.
- Director approval above 500,000 is rejected unless a valid manager first-stage approval has already been recorded.
- Approvals must enforce the userΓÇÖs role and preserve the invoice when rejected.
- Rejected attempts must maintain the previous `Status`, approving records, timestamps, and decision history unchanged.

Planned tests:
- Manager can approve exactly 50,000.
- Manager cannot approve 50,001.
- Director can approve exactly 500,000.
- Director cannot approve amounts above 500,000 without a manager stage.
- Non-director role attempts are rejected with a clear reason and no mutation.

### Phase 2: Two-stage approval flow above 500,000

Goal: enforce the required manager-first, different-director-second flow and separation of duties.

Planned domain behavior:
- Introduce explicit staged state tracking in the domain model (or an equivalent minimal structure in the domain layer) that records stage progress without ambiguity.
- Require a manager stage before any director finalization above 500,000.
- Reject same-user attempts that would satisfy both stages.
- Reject out-of-order or incomplete stage attempts.
- Preserve the earlier stage record if the final director stage is not valid.

Planned tests:
- Manager first-stage approval then different director second-stage approval succeeds.
- Second-stage approval before first-stage approval is rejected.
- Same-user stage completion is rejected.
- Missing first-stage approval leaves invoice pending and unchanged.
- Repeated decision attempts after final outcome remain rejected without mutation.

### Phase 3: API and UI verification

Goal: validate contract-level behavior through the existing Web API and role enforcement model.

Planned validation:
- Keep controllers thin and preserve `ApiControllerBase` and `RequireRole` conventions in [backend/src/InvoiceApp.Api/Controllers/ApprovalsController.cs](backend/src/InvoiceApp.Api/Controllers/ApprovalsController.cs).
- Ensure the API surfaces clear failure messages without embedding approval logic in the controller layer.
- Reuse the current session-based user identity for role checks and clear rejection reasons.

Planned tests:
- Add or adjust Playwright flow coverage in [e2e/tests](e2e/tests) and the corresponding page objects in [e2e/pages](e2e/pages) to cover the manager and director approval path.
- Validate the final approval scenario with a manager + different director for `> 500,000` invoices.
- Validate failure paths: wrong role, missing stage, blank reason, final decision already made.

### Phase 4: Mutation testing and final verification

Goal: prove the approval invariants survive code mutations and the repo's standard validation still passes.

Required tooling plan:
- Pin the repo-approved Stryker.NET version in the tool manifest or local dev setup before running mutation testing.
- Run the mutation suite against the domain project so only meaningful approval rules are evaluated.
- Treat surviving mutants as a signal to add or tighten tests before accepting the feature.

Verification commands:
- `dotnet test backend/InvoiceApp.sln`
- `cd e2e && npm install && npx playwright install chromium && npm test`
- `dotnet tool restore` followed by `dotnet stryker` (or the repoΓÇÖs pinned equivalent command using the approved Stryker.NET version)

Acceptance gate:
- All xUnit tests pass.
- Playwright tests pass for the approval scenarios.
- Mutation testing shows no critical approval-rule mutants survive without a corresponding test.

## Assumptions and Risks

### Assumptions
- The current in-memory session model and role attributes remain the source of truth for authorization.
- Existing approval state is a domain concern and should not be handled by ad hoc UI or controller logic.
- A rejected approval is a no-op: if any invoice field related to approval state changes, the attempt is non-compliant.
- The threshold logic is based on the feature spec and not on hidden or undocumented exceptions.

### Risks
- Risk: stage state may be under-modeled if the domain only tracks the final decision and not the stage history. Mitigation: capture explicit stage progression in the domain model and test the preserved history.
- Risk: controller logic could accidentally duplicate business rules. Mitigation: keep approval checks in `ApprovalService` and use controller methods only to pass user identity and request input.
- Risk: role enforcement could drift from the existing auth model. Mitigation: review the existing auth middleware and RequiredRole usage before finalizing the API layer and Playwright path.
- Risk: mutation testing can identify gaps in domain coverage. Mitigation: require a test for each mutant-relevant invariant before considering the feature complete.

## AGENTS.md and repo governance updates

This feature does not require new project architecture, but the project guidance should be reinforced to say:
- approval rule enforcement stays in the domain project,
- every new rule must be backed by a failing xUnit test,
- the mutation-test command is part of the verification workflow,
- and the role-based authorization model remains fixed while the approval logic evolves.

If the repo chooses to enforce the mutation-test tool version in project documentation, the command examples in AGENTS.md should be updated to reflect the approved Stryker.NET version rather than a floating package reference.

## Complexity Tracking

No constitution violations are expected for this feature. The design reuses the existing project structure and keeps the change within the established domain-layer and auth conventions.

## Implementation Phases

### Phase 0: Test-first domain specification

Goal: lock down the approval invariants before any production code changes.

Planned work:
- Add failing unit tests in [backend/tests/InvoiceApp.Tests/ApprovalServiceTests.cs](backend/tests/InvoiceApp.Tests/ApprovalServiceTests.cs) for the exact threshold boundaries.
- Cover the manager single-stage path at 50,000 and 50,001.
- Cover the director single-stage path at 500,000 and above 500,000 without the required manager stage.
- Cover invalid-role attempts and blank rejection reasons.
- Cover same-user stage attempts and out-of-order stage attempts for the >500,000 flow.

Exit criteria:
- Tests fail before implementation because the new business rules are not yet present.
- Each test names the exact invariant it protects.
- No rule is accepted without a failing test demonstrating the expected behavior.

### Phase 1: Single-stage approval rules

Goal: implement the path for manager and director approvals that do not require a second stage.

Planned logic in `ApprovalService`:
- Manager approval is valid for amounts `<= 50,000` and rejected above 50,000.
- Director approval is valid for amounts `> 50,000` and `<= 500,000`.
- Director approval above 500,000 is rejected unless a valid manager first-stage approval has already been recorded.
- Approvals must enforce the userΓÇÖs role and preserve the invoice when rejected.
- Rejected attempts must maintain the previous `Status`, approving records, timestamps, and decision history unchanged.

Planned tests:
- Manager can approve exactly 50,000.
- Manager cannot approve 50,001.
- Director can approve exactly 500,000.
- Director cannot approve amounts above 500,000 without a manager stage.
- Non-director role attempts are rejected with a clear reason and no mutation.

### Phase 2: Two-stage approval flow above 500,000

Goal: enforce the required manager-first, different-director-second flow and separation of duties.

Planned domain behavior:
- Introduce explicit staged state tracking in the domain model (or an equivalent minimal structure in the domain layer) that records stage progress without ambiguity.
- Require a manager stage before any director finalization above 500,000.
- Reject same-user attempts that would satisfy both stages.
- Reject out-of-order or incomplete stage attempts.
- Preserve the earlier stage record if the final director stage is not valid.

Planned tests:
- Manager first-stage approval then different director second-stage approval succeeds.
- Second-stage approval before first-stage approval is rejected.
- Same-user stage completion is rejected.
- Missing first-stage approval leaves invoice pending and unchanged.
- Repeated decision attempts after final outcome remain rejected without mutation.

### Phase 3: API and UI verification

Goal: validate contract-level behavior through the existing Web API and role enforcement model.

Planned validation:
- Keep controllers thin and preserve `ApiControllerBase` and `RequireRole` conventions in [backend/src/InvoiceApp.Api/Controllers/ApprovalsController.cs](backend/src/InvoiceApp.Api/Controllers/ApprovalsController.cs).
- Ensure the API surfaces clear failure messages without embedding approval logic in the controller layer.
- Reuse the current session-based user identity for role checks and clear rejection reasons.

Planned tests:
- Add or adjust Playwright flow coverage in [e2e/tests](e2e/tests) and the corresponding page objects in [e2e/pages](e2e/pages) to cover the manager and director approval path.
- Validate the final approval scenario with a manager + different director for `> 500,000` invoices.
- Validate failure paths: wrong role, missing stage, blank reason, final decision already made.

### Phase 4: Mutation testing and final verification

Goal: prove the approval invariants survive code mutations and the repo's standard validation still passes.

Required tooling plan:
- Pin the repo-approved Stryker.NET version in the tool manifest or local dev setup before running mutation testing.
- Run the mutation suite against the domain project so only meaningful approval rules are evaluated.
- Treat surviving mutants as a signal to add or tighten tests before accepting the feature.

Verification commands:
- `dotnet test backend/InvoiceApp.sln`
- `cd e2e && npm install && npx playwright install chromium && npm test`
- `dotnet tool restore` followed by `dotnet stryker` (or the repoΓÇÖs pinned equivalent command using the approved Stryker.NET version)

Acceptance gate:
- All xUnit tests pass.
- Playwright tests pass for the approval scenarios.
- Mutation testing shows no critical approval-rule mutants survive without a corresponding test.

## Assumptions and Risks

### Assumptions
- The current in-memory session model and role attributes remain the source of truth for authorization.
- Existing approval state is a domain concern and should not be handled by ad hoc UI or controller logic.
- A rejected approval is a no-op: if any invoice field related to approval state changes, the attempt is non-compliant.
- The threshold logic is based on the feature spec and not on hidden or undocumented exceptions.

### Risks
- Risk: stage state may be under-modeled if the domain only tracks the final decision and not the stage history. Mitigation: capture explicit stage progression in the domain model and test the preserved history.
- Risk: controller logic could accidentally duplicate business rules. Mitigation: keep approval checks in `ApprovalService` and use controller methods only to pass user identity and request input.
- Risk: role enforcement could drift from the existing auth model. Mitigation: review the existing auth middleware and RequiredRole usage before finalizing the API layer and Playwright path.
- Risk: mutation testing can identify gaps in domain coverage. Mitigation: require a test for each mutant-relevant invariant before considering the feature complete.

## AGENTS.md and repo governance updates

This feature does not require new project architecture, but the project guidance should be reinforced to say:
- approval rule enforcement stays in the domain project,
- every new rule must be backed by a failing xUnit test,
- the mutation-test command is part of the verification workflow,
- and the role-based authorization model remains fixed while the approval logic evolves.

If the repo chooses to enforce the mutation-test tool version in project documentation, the command examples in AGENTS.md should be updated to reflect the approved Stryker.NET version rather than a floating package reference.

## Complexity Tracking

No constitution violations are expected for this feature. The design reuses the existing project structure and keeps the change within the established domain-layer and auth conventions.

**Input**: User description: "Managers may finally approve invoices up to 50,000. Directors may finally approve invoices up to 500,000. For invoices above 500,000, a Manager provides the first-stage approval, and a different Director provides the second-stage approval that finalizes the invoice. The same user cannot satisfy both approval stages. Invalid approval attempts must return a clear reason and leave the invoice unchanged."
### User Story 1 - Routine invoice approval by a manager (Priority: P1)

A manager needs to finalize an invoice that is within the manager approval limit without escalating to a director. The workflow must be clear, auditable, and easy to verify when the amount is at the threshold boundary.
**Why this priority**: This is the primary business path for daily invoice processing and must behave correctly at exact threshold boundaries before any exception path is considered.
**Independent Test**: A manager can finalize an invoice exactly at the manager limit and the invoice records a clear final decision without ambiguity.
1. **Given** an invoice in Pending Approval with an amount of exactly 50,000, **When** a manager submits a final approval, **Then** the invoice is approved and the approving manager is recorded.

2. **Given** an invoice in Pending Approval with an amount of 50,001, **When** a manager submits a final approval, **Then** the request is rejected with a clear reason and the invoice remains unchanged.
3. **Given** an invoice in Pending Approval with an amount below 50,000, **When** a manager submits a final approval, **Then** the invoice is approved as the managerΓÇÖs final decision.
### User Story 2 - Director approval for larger invoices (Priority: P1)

A director needs to finalize invoices that are within the director approval limit. The process must ensure that only the correct role can decide at that threshold and that invalid role attempts are rejected without mutating the invoice.
**Why this priority**: Director approvals involve larger values and require explicit role enforcement to avoid unauthorized final decisions.
**Independent Test**: A director can finalize an invoice at 500,000, while non-director users or out-of-range approvals are rejected with a clear reason and no invoice mutation.

1. **Given** an invoice in Pending Approval with an amount of exactly 500,000, **When** a director submits a final approval, **Then** the invoice is approved and the director is recorded as the final approver.

2. **Given** an invoice in Pending Approval with an amount above 500,000, **When** a director attempts a final approval without the required first-stage manager approval, **Then** the request is rejected with a clear reason and the invoice remains unchanged.

3. **Given** an invoice in Pending Approval with an amount above 500,000, **When** a user without the Director role attempts the final approval, **Then** the request is rejected with a clear reason and no invoice fields are changed.
### User Story 3 - Multi-stage approval for very large invoices (Priority: P1)

A very large invoice requires a two-stage approval path: a manager completes the first stage, and a different director completes the second stage to finalize the invoice. The same user cannot satisfy both stages, and rejected attempts must not alter approval history.
**Why this priority**: This is the highest-risk approval scenario, and it requires explicit separation of duties and strict state preservation to prevent invalid progression.

**Independent Test**: A manager and a different director can complete the required stages for a large invoice, while same-user, missing-stage, or out-of-order stage attempts are rejected without mutation.

1. **Given** an invoice above 500,000 that is pending a two-stage approval flow, **When** a manager records the first-stage approval and a different director records the second-stage final approval, **Then** the invoice is finalized successfully and the stage history reflects the two different approvers.

2. **Given** an invoice above 500,000, **When** a second-stage approval is attempted before the first-stage manager approval is recorded, **Then** the attempt is rejected with a clear reason and the invoice remains unchanged.

3. **Given** an invoice above 500,000, **When** the same user attempts to satisfy both stages, **Then** the second-stage attempt is rejected and the invoiceΓÇÖs status, stage records, final approver, decision timestamp, and decision note history remain unchanged.

4. **Given** an invoice above 500,000, **When** the required manager stage is recorded but a different director fails to complete final approval, **Then** the invoice remains pending and the prior stage record remains intact until a valid final approval is submitted.
### User Story 4 - Invalid approval attempts, lifecycle errors, and state preservation (Priority: P2)

An approver needs immediate feedback whenever the approval action is invalid. The system must explain the reason, preserve the invoice state, and keep rejection behavior distinct from approval so the business can correct the action confidently.

**Why this priority**: Invalid approval attempts are high-risk from a governance perspective because they can create confusion, duplicate decisions, or silent state drift if they are not clearly blocked.
**Independent Test**: Approval and rejection attempts that do not meet the current lifecycle, role, or data requirements are rejected without mutating the invoiceΓÇÖs recorded state.

1. **Given** an invoice that is not in Pending Approval, **When** an approver attempts to approve or reject it, **Then** the system rejects the attempt with a clear reason and preserves the invoiceΓÇÖs status, approver, timestamp, and decision note history.

2. **Given** an invoice that has already received a final approval or rejection, **When** a repeated approval or rejection attempt is submitted, **Then** the system rejects the attempt and leaves the invoice decision unchanged.
3. **Given** an invoice pending approval, **When** a user submits a rejection without a reason, **Then** the system rejects the rejection without saving a decision or mutating the invoice.

4. **Given** a user without the required role for the current stage, **When** they attempt to complete that approval stage, **Then** the action is rejected with a clear reason and no invoice fields are changed.

5. **Given** a rejected approval attempt, **When** the system evaluates the resulting state, **Then** the invoice retains the same status, approval-stage records, final approver, decision timestamp, and decision note/history that existed before the rejected attempt.
- Exact threshold values are accepted only where the rule allows them: a Manager final approval is valid at 50,000, and a Director final approval is valid at 500,000.

- Amounts above the manager threshold are rejected for Manager final approval; amounts above the director threshold are rejected for Director final approval unless the required Manager first-stage approval has already been recorded.
- Invoices above 500,000 follow the two-stage rule: a Manager must complete stage one, a different Director must complete stage two, and the same user cannot satisfy both stages.

- Any rejected approval or rejection attempt leaves the invoice unchanged, including status, approval-stage records, final approver, decision timestamp, and decision note/history that existed before the rejected attempt.

- Repeated decisions after a final outcome has already been recorded, out-of-order stage attempts, invalid-role attempts, and blank rejection reasons are rejected without mutating the invoice or its existing approval history.
- **FR-001**: The system MUST allow a Manager to provide a final approval for an invoice of exactly 50,000.
- **FR-002**: The system MUST allow a Director to provide a final approval for any invoice above 50,000 and up to and including 500,000.
- **FR-003**: The system MUST reject a Manager final approval attempt for any invoice above 50,000.
- **FR-004**: The system MUST reject a Director final approval attempt for any invoice above 500,000 unless the required Manager first-stage approval has already been recorded.
- **FR-005**: The system MUST require a Manager first-stage approval before a Director can finalize an invoice above 500,000.
- **FR-006**: The system MUST require a different approver identity for the final Director stage than the Manager who completed the earlier stage.
- **FR-007**: The system MUST reject any approval attempt where the same user would satisfy both approval stages for the same invoice.
- **FR-008**: The system MUST reject any approval attempt by users without the required role for that stage, with a clear reason and no invoice mutation.
- **FR-009**: The system MUST reject approval attempts against invoices that are not in Pending Approval without mutating the invoice.
- **FR-010**: The system MUST reject repeated approval or rejection attempts after a final decision has already been recorded without changing the recorded decision.
- **FR-011**: The system MUST reject any rejection attempt that does not include a valid reason without saving the decision.

- **FR-012**: For any rejected approval or rejection attempt, the system MUST preserve the invoiceΓÇÖs status, approval-stage records, final approver, decision timestamp, and decision note/history that existed before the rejected attempt.
- **FR-013**: The system MUST maintain a clear distinction between approval and rejection outcomes so that final states remain unambiguous.
- **FR-014**: The system MUST preserve the existing authentication and authorization model while enforcing the approval workflow rules.
### Key Entities *(include if feature involves data)*
- **Invoice**: The business record being reviewed, including amount, status, approval stages, and decision history.
- **Approver**: A person or role-based actor who can take part in an approval action.
- **Approval Stage**: A specific step in the approval sequence, including the Manager first-stage approval and the Director final-stage approval.
- **Approval Decision**: The final outcome of the invoice review, including approval, rejection, the actor, and the reason when applicable.
- **SC-001**: 100% of Manager final approval attempts at 50,000 are accepted, and 100% of Manager final approval attempts above 50,000 are rejected with a clear reason and no invoice mutation.

- **SC-002**: 100% of Director final approval attempts at 500,000 are accepted, and 100% of Director final approval attempts above 500,000 are rejected unless a valid Manager first-stage approval has already been recorded.
- **SC-003**: 100% of approval flows above 500,000 require a Manager first-stage approval and a different Director second-stage approval before finalization occurs.
- **SC-004**: 100% of same-user, out-of-order, or missing-stage approval attempts are rejected, and the invoice remains unchanged for every rejected attempt.

- **SC-005**: 100% of invalid-role approval attempts are rejected with a clear reason and do not modify the invoice status, stage records, final approver, decision timestamp, or decision note/history.
- **SC-006**: 100% of repeated approval attempts after a final decision and blank rejection attempts are rejected without changing the recorded decision.
- **SC-007**: Users can understand the approval outcome and the reason for rejection without inspecting hidden implementation details or backend state not exposed by the workflow rules.
- The approval policy is defined by the projectΓÇÖs business rules rather than by ad hoc controller logic.
- Existing role-based authentication and authorization rules remain in effect for all approval actions.
- Approval decisions are evaluated against the invoice amount and current status before any approval is accepted.

- A rejected approval attempt is considered unsuccessful only when the invoice state remains unchanged in all fields relevant to approval status, stage records, final approver, decision timestamp, and decision note/history.
- The detailed feature specification may refine the user-facing labels and messages, but the approval invariants remain non-negotiable.
- The system can be reviewed and validated through the existing unit and workflow test conventions already used in the repository.

The invoice lifecycle, approval transitions, threshold checks, and state mutations MUST live in InvoiceApp.Domain, especially in ApprovalService. API controllers and UI code MAY accept input and display outcomes, but they MUST NOT define business rules or decide whether an invoice is valid to approve.
This preserves the existing architecture and makes the approval policy explicit, reviewable, and testable without coupling business logic to the web layer.

Every business rule and boundary condition MUST have meaningful unit tests before implementation is considered complete. AI-generated tests are not accepted as proof of correctness unless the tests are reviewed for rule coverage and the code would fail if the relevant invariant were violated.

The projectΓÇÖs xUnit suite is the primary enforcement mechanism for domain behavior, and any new approval rule must be expressed as a testable invariant rather than an inferred implementation detail.

Approval logic MUST be explicit, testable, and invariant-based. Invoices must produce clear, reviewable approval outcomes for manager and director flows, multi-stage approval, distinct approver identities, and rejection without invoice mutation.

The detailed approval thresholds and stage sequencing are left to the feature specification, but the implementation MUST preserve these invariants: managers may finally approve invoices up to 50,000; directors may finally approve invoices up to 500,000; for amounts above 500,000, a manager provides the first-stage approval and a different director provides the second-stage final approval; the same user cannot satisfy both approval stages; and invalid approval attempts return a clear reason and leave the invoice unchanged.

All API behavior MUST preserve the existing authentication, role-based authorization, and error-mapping conventions in InvoiceApp.Api. Controllers must continue to inherit from ApiControllerBase, use the established Handle(...) flow for service errors, and remain behind sign-in and role enforcement.
This prevents drift between the contract and the security model and keeps the demo consistent with the repositoryΓÇÖs intended architecture.

Changes MUST reuse the existing domain/service boundaries, repository conventions, and test patterns. The project must avoid unnecessary dependencies, unrelated refactoring, or broader architecture churn when a small, reviewable change will satisfy the requirement.
This protects the demoΓÇÖs simplicity and makes the repo easier to reason about during AI-in-SDLC exercises and reviews.

Before any rule is treated as accepted, the project MUST run dotnet test backend/InvoiceApp.sln, review the resulting diff, and document findings rather than assuming generated code is correct. Fresh evidence is the default standard for accepting behavior changes.
A change is not validated by generation alone; it is validated when the relevant tests and review artifacts demonstrate the rule is enforced in the codebase.
The invoice approval demo MUST remain aligned with the following standards:
- InvoiceApp.Domain owns business rules and repository contracts; InvoiceApp.Api owns controllers, authentication, and UI assets.
- Repositories are interfaces in the domain project with in-memory implementations in the API project for local, single-process execution.
- Controllers MUST inherit from ApiControllerBase and route using the conventional api/<controller> pattern.
- Request records are declared in the controller and used only to shape API input; no business logic is allowed there.
- Every approval rule and boundary condition MUST be covered by a test that would fail if the rule were violated.
- Approval thresholds and multi-stage paths must be explicit in the feature specification and validated with tests before completion.
- Invalid approval attempts MUST return a clear reason and leave the invoice unchanged; no mutation is allowed on a rejected approval attempt.
- Naming MUST be explicit and readable; one-letter variables and vague flag parameters are prohibited.
- Demo credentials are for local use only and MUST never be treated as real production credentials or committed as sensitive secrets.
Changes to this project MUST follow the repository workflow described in AGENTS.md and the project README:
- Business rules are implemented in the domain project before the API layer is updated.
- Authentication and authorization requirements are enforced before endpoints are considered complete.
- Tests are required for every new rule, endpoint, or regression fix.
- Manual verification is expected for the approval flow and role behavior when a user-facing change is made.
- Pull requests and code review MUST confirm that the change respects the domain boundary, the role model, and the projectΓÇÖs simple architecture.
This Constitution supersedes informal practices for this repository. All project changes MUST be evaluated against it before being considered complete.

Amendments require a clear rationale, updated versioning, and a review of the impacted principles and workflow sections. The project MUST record the change in this constitution, note the reason for the amendment, and retain a traceable history of the decision.

Versioning MUST follow semantic versioning: MAJOR changes remove or redefine governance rules in a backward-incompatible way, MINOR changes add or materially expand a principle or section, and PATCH changes clarify wording or refine non-semantic guidance. A change that adds a governance requirement or materially narrows allowed behavior is a MAJOR or MINOR change based on impact.

Compliance review is mandatory before a change is considered ready. Reviewers MUST verify that the behavior, tests, and documentation remain aligned with the domain rule, the role model, and the projectΓÇÖs simplicity standard.

children.text: This feature adds explicit approval thresholds and separation-of-duties rules for invoices in the existing ASP.NET Core demo. The implementation must keep the invoice lifecycle and approval invariants in the domain layer so the API layer remains a thin adapter over a validated business service. The work is split into two stages: first the single-stage manager/director decision rules at 50,000 and 500,000, then the two-stage path for amounts above 500,000, with unit tests driving each rule and a Playwright workflow test validating the end-user flow.
**Primary Dependencies**: xUnit, Playwright, existing in-memory repository and session-based role auth
**Storage**: In-memory repository in the API project; domain contracts remain interface-based and repository-agnostic
**Testing**: xUnit for domain/unit tests; Playwright for end-to-end role-based workflow validation; Stryker.NET for mutation testing using the repo-approved pinned version
**Target Platform**: Local demo web app and automated tests in the repository workspace
**Project Type**: Web service + static UI demo
**Performance Goals**: no throughput target beyond synchronous local demo behavior; correctness and state preservation are the primary constraints
**Constraints**: approval rules must remain in InvoiceApp.Domain; controllers must not encode business logic; all rejected attempts must preserve state; existing auth/session model must remain intact
**Scale/Scope**: small demo app with a single invoice approval workflow and a small set of role-based scenarios
*Gate status: PASS before implementation, with explicit compliance checks to re-run after design and before completion.*
- Business logic stays in InvoiceApp.Domain; controllers remain request shapers and keep using ApiControllerBase and RequireRole enforcement.
- Test-first development is enforced by adding failing xUnit tests for each approval threshold and invalid-attempt case before implementation.
- Approval correctness is preserved through explicit threshold checks, separation-of-duties rules, and no-mutation semantics for rejected attempts.
- API and security consistency remains intact because session-based role enforcement continues to live in the existing auth model.
- Minimal scope is maintained by reusing the existing ApprovalService, repository contract, and test patterns rather than introducing new abstractions or unrelated refactoring.
- Verification is required through `dotnet test backend/InvoiceApp.sln`, Playwright validation, and mutation testing before considering the feature complete.
